title: Biochar carbon removal

definition.text: A negative emissions method that turns leftover biomass into biochar by pyrolysis and stores it in soil or durable materials; also called pyrogenic carbon capture and storage.

facts.text: Plants take CO2 from the air as they grow; pyrolysis locks that carbon into a stable form that can last centuries to millennia.
Biomass is heated to 350–900 °C with little oxygen, giving biochar plus bio-oil and pyrogas.
In 2022/2023 it accounted for 87–92% of all delivered carbon removals.
Its potential is put at 0.3 to 4.9 billion tonnes of CO2 per year.
It is seen as quick to deploy and capital-efficient, suited to farmers and rural diversification in developing countries.
Some studies report fast decay or more soil emissions, though a 2025 re-analysis says common decay models overestimate decay.

contested_note: Studies disagree on how fast biochar carbon decays in soil, partly because of disputed decay models.

definition.text: Carbon credits earned by certified biochar carbon removal and sold in carbon markets.

facts.text: Because abatement costs are high, biochar credits trade about an order of magnitude above credits from emission cuts or nature-based solutions.
In 2024 biochar projects made up 86% of the volume of carbon dioxide removal purchases.
To be certified, suppliers must be carbon net-negative, storing more carbon than they use making and distributing biochar.

title: Bioenergy with carbon capture and storage
article: Bioenergy with carbon capture and storage

definition.text: Getting energy from biomass and capturing and storing the carbon dioxide this produces; known as BECCS.

facts.text: Growing plants absorb CO2; when their energy is used, some CO2 is captured and stored underground, so BECCS can remove CO2 from the air under some conditions.
Its negative emissions potential has been estimated at zero to 22 gigatonnes a year.
Cost estimates range from $60 to $250 per ton of CO2.
As of 2024 only 3 large-scale BECCS projects operated worldwide.
Large-scale biomass growing risks breaching planetary boundaries through land and water scarcity, biodiversity loss, competition with food and deforestation.
Using farm and forestry residues instead of energy crops avoids many of these problems.

title: Carbon capture technologies
article: Bioenergy with carbon capture and storage#Technology

definition.text: The three main ways to capture CO2 from burning fuel: post-combustion, pre-combustion and oxy-fuel combustion.

facts.text: Post-combustion separates CO2 from flue gas after burning and can be retrofitted to existing plants.
Pre-combustion gasifies fuel into syngas and captures CO2 before power is made.
Oxy-fuel combustion burns fuel in oxygen and recycled flue gas, giving a CO2-rich exhaust.
Expected efficiencies are 95% for post-combustion, 85% for pre-combustion and 87.5% for oxy-combustion.

related: Bioenergy with carbon capture and storage

definition.text: A family of carbon removal methods that collect biomass, such as farm waste, and store its carbon permanently or semi-permanently; known as BiCRS.

facts.text: Unlike direct air capture, which is costly and energy-hungry, it relies on photosynthesis and then engineering to store the carbon-rich residue.
It includes BECCS and biochar carbon removal.
Challenges include measuring the carbon stored in buried biomass and extra demand for farmland, so think tanks urge limits on which biomass may be used.
